topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Which federal agency insures FHA loans made by approved private lenders to reduce lender risk on qualifying home loans?
choice_a: The Federal Housing Administration (a division of HUD)
choice_b: The Federal Reserve Board
choice_c: The Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae)
choice_d: The Farm Service Agency
explanation: FHA, part of HUD, insures loans made by FHA-approved lenders, protecting the lender against borrower default; FHA does not originate loans directly.
source_note: 12 U.S.C. § 1709; National Housing Act of 1934; HUD FHA single-family program.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A qualified borrower with a credit score of 580 or higher applying for an FHA-insured loan is generally required to make a minimum down payment of what amount?
explanation: FHA allows a minimum down payment of 3.5% for borrowers with credit scores of 580 or higher; lower scores generally require a higher (10%) down payment.
source_note: HUD Handbook 4000.1, FHA Single Family Housing Policy Handbook.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: FHA-insured loans require borrowers to pay for mortgage insurance in what two forms?
choice_a: A one-time hazard insurance premium only
choice_b: Private mortgage insurance (PMI) paid monthly only
choice_c: An upfront mortgage insurance premium (UFMIP) and an annual mortgage insurance premium (MIP)
choice_d: A funding fee paid at closing only
explanation: FHA loans require an upfront mortgage insurance premium (typically financed into the loan) plus an ongoing annual MIP collected as part of the monthly payment.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: One of the primary advantages of a VA-guaranteed home loan for an eligible veteran is:
choice_a: A federally mandated interest rate cap of 3%
choice_b: Automatic forgiveness of the loan after 10 years
choice_c: Exemption from all state real estate transfer taxes
choice_d: The elimination of a down payment requirement in most cases
explanation: VA loans, guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs, typically allow qualified veterans to finance up to 100% of the purchase price with no down payment.
source_note: 38 U.S.C. Chapter 37; VA Lenders Handbook (VA Pamphlet 26-7).

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The one-time fee charged on most VA-guaranteed loans to help offset the cost of the program to taxpayers is known as the:
choice_a: VA funding fee
choice_b: Guarantee fee
choice_c: Origination premium
choice_d: Upfront mortgage insurance premium
explanation: The VA funding fee is paid by most borrowers (with exemptions for veterans receiving service-connected disability compensation) and can be financed into the loan.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Before a lender can process a VA loan, the veteran borrower must first obtain a document from the VA verifying eligibility for the benefit, called a:
choice_a: Certificate of Reasonable Value
choice_b: Certificate of Eligibility (COE)
choice_c: Loan Guaranty Certificate
choice_d: Discharge Verification Letter
explanation: The Certificate of Eligibility, obtained from the VA, confirms the veteran's entitlement amount and eligibility for the VA loan guaranty program.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: USDA Rural Development guaranteed home loans are restricted to properties located in designated rural areas and to borrowers who:
choice_a: Are active-duty military only
choice_b: Have a minimum down payment of 20%
choice_c: Meet income limits, generally not exceeding 115% of the area median income
choice_d: Purchase only agricultural land used for farming
explanation: The USDA Section 502 Guaranteed Rural Housing Loan Program requires the property to be in an eligible rural area and household income to fall within published limits, generally up to 115% of area median income.
source_note: 7 U.S.C. § 1927; USDA Rural Development Handbook HB-1-3555.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Like VA loans, USDA guaranteed loans typically require no down payment, but they charge borrowers a comparable cost known as the:
choice_a: Private mortgage insurance premium
choice_b: Discount points
choice_c: Impound surcharge
choice_d: Guarantee fee (upfront and annual)
explanation: USDA guaranteed loans charge an upfront guarantee fee (financeable into the loan) and an annual fee in lieu of traditional mortgage insurance.
source_note: USDA Rural Development Handbook HB-1-3555, Chapter 16.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The primary purpose of the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) is to:
choice_a: Protect consumers by requiring disclosure of settlement costs and prohibiting kickbacks for referrals of settlement services
choice_b: Set maximum commission rates brokers may charge
choice_c: Guarantee a fixed interest rate for all federally related mortgages
choice_d: Require lenders to approve loans within 24 hours
explanation: RESPA (1974), implemented by Regulation X and enforced by the CFPB, is designed to help consumers become better shoppers for settlement services and to eliminate abusive practices such as kickbacks.
source_note: 12 U.S.C. § 2601 et seq.; Regulation X, 12 CFR Part 1024.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under Section 8 of RESPA, which of the following is prohibited?
choice_a: Charging any fee at all for title insurance
choice_b: Giving or accepting a fee, kickback, or thing of value in exchange for the referral of settlement service business
choice_c: Using an attorney to close a transaction
choice_d: Disclosing the identity of the loan servicer
explanation: RESPA Section 8 prohibits kickbacks, referral fees, and unearned fee splitting related to federally related mortgage loan settlement services.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A title company and a real estate brokerage may legally form an affiliated business arrangement (AfBA) under RESPA's Section 8 exception only if:
choice_a: The arrangement is kept confidential from consumers
choice_b: The brokerage receives a flat referral fee regardless of services performed
choice_c: The referring party discloses the relationship in writing, the consumer is not required to use the affiliate, and any fee received reflects services actually performed
choice_d: Only licensed attorneys may participate
explanation: The AfBA exception under RESPA requires a written disclosure of the ownership interest, freedom for the consumer to choose another provider, and that payments received are only for goods, facilities, or services actually furnished.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: RESPA generally applies to:
choice_a: Any loan of any kind made by any lender
choice_b: Only cash real estate transactions with no financing
choice_c: Commercial loans over $1 million only
choice_d: Federally related mortgage loans secured by a lien on residential property of one to four units
explanation: RESPA's coverage is limited to "federally related mortgage loans" — loans secured by a lien on residential real property designed for one-to-four families.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: At the time of loan application, RESPA requires the lender to provide the borrower with a disclosure statement addressing:
choice_a: Whether the loan servicing may be sold, assigned, or transferred during the life of the loan
choice_b: The exact resale value of the home in five years
choice_c: The broker's commission split
choice_d: The buyer's credit score
explanation: The Servicing Disclosure Statement informs applicants whether the lender intends to service the loan or may transfer or sell the servicing rights.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under RESPA's escrow account provisions, a loan servicer may generally require an escrow cushion of no more than:
choice_a: One full year of payments
choice_b: One-sixth (2 months) of the estimated total annual disbursements
choice_c: 50% of the loan balance
choice_d: There is no limit on escrow cushions
explanation: RESPA Section 10 and Regulation X limit the escrow cushion to an amount not exceeding one-sixth of the estimated total annual escrow disbursements (roughly a two-month cushion).

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Primary federal regulatory and enforcement authority over RESPA currently rests with the:
choice_a: Department of Veterans Affairs
choice_b: Federal Trade Commission exclusively
choice_c: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
choice_d: National Association of REALTORS®
explanation: Since the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, RESPA rulemaking and primary enforcement authority transferred from HUD to the CFPB.
source_note: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, 12 U.S.C. § 5481 et seq.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under Section 9 of RESPA, a seller in a real estate transaction involving a federally related mortgage loan is prohibited from:
choice_a: Choosing their own listing agent
choice_b: Negotiating the sale price
choice_c: Paying any portion of the buyer's closing costs
choice_d: Requiring the buyer, as a condition of sale, to purchase title insurance from a particular title company
explanation: RESPA Section 9 prohibits sellers from conditioning a sale on the buyer's use of a specific title insurance company; violators are liable to the buyer for up to three times all title insurance charges.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: If a borrower believes their loan servicer made an error in handling their mortgage account, RESPA gives the borrower the right to send a formal written inquiry called a:
choice_a: Qualified Written Request (QWR)
choice_b: Notice of Default
choice_c: Truth-in-Lending Rescission Notice
choice_d: Loan Estoppel Certificate
explanation: A Qualified Written Request under RESPA requires the servicer to acknowledge and investigate the borrower's inquiry and respond within specified timeframes.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Before the 2015 TRID rule consolidated disclosures, RESPA required which standardized form itemizing all settlement charges at closing for most mortgage transactions?
choice_a: The Uniform Residential Loan Application
choice_b: The HUD-1 Settlement Statement
choice_c: The Good Faith Estimate only
choice_d: IRS Form 1099-S
explanation: Prior to TRID, RESPA required use of the HUD-1 (or HUD-1A) Settlement Statement itemizing all charges to buyer and seller; it has since been replaced by the Closing Disclosure for most loans.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The primary goal of the Truth in Lending Act (TILA) is to:
choice_a: Set the maximum commission a broker may earn
choice_b: Require all loans to have a fixed interest rate
choice_c: Ensure consumers receive meaningful, standardized disclosure of credit terms, including the annual percentage rate (APR), so they can compare loan costs
choice_d: Regulate the appraisal profession
explanation: TILA (1968), implemented through Regulation Z, requires standardized disclosure of the cost of credit, most notably the APR, to promote informed comparison shopping.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1601 et seq.; Regulation Z, 12 CFR Part 1026.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The TRID rule, effective October 2015, combined which two federal disclosure sets into the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms?
choice_a: FHA and VA disclosures
choice_b: Fair Housing Act and ADA disclosures
choice_c: CERCLA and lead-paint disclosures
choice_d: TILA disclosures and RESPA (GFE/HUD-1) disclosures
explanation: The TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure (TRID) rule merged the early Truth-in-Lending disclosure and the RESPA Good Faith Estimate into the Loan Estimate, and the final TIL statement and HUD-1 into the Closing Disclosure.
source_note: 12 CFR Part 1026, Subpart E (TRID Rule, CFPB final rule effective 10/3/2015).

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under TRID, a lender must provide the consumer with the Loan Estimate no later than:
choice_a: 3 business days after receiving the consumer's loan application
choice_b: At closing
choice_c: 30 days after application
choice_d: Only upon the consumer's specific written request
explanation: Regulation Z requires the Loan Estimate be delivered or placed in the mail within three business days of receiving a completed loan application.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: TRID requires that the consumer receive the Closing Disclosure at least how many business days before loan consummation (closing)?
choice_a: 1 business day
choice_b: 3 business days
choice_c: 7 business days
choice_d: 10 business days
explanation: Regulation Z requires that the Closing Disclosure be received by the borrower at least three business days before consummation of a closed-end mortgage loan.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: TILA's three-business-day right of rescission applies to:
choice_a: Purchase-money mortgages used to buy a primary residence
choice_b: All commercial real estate loans
choice_c: Certain refinance and home equity loans secured by the borrower's principal dwelling
choice_d: VA-guaranteed purchase loans only
explanation: The TILA right of rescission generally allows a borrower three business days to cancel certain refinances or home equity loans on their principal residence; it does not apply to purchase-money mortgages.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The Annual Percentage Rate (APR) disclosed under TILA differs from the note (contract) interest rate because the APR:
choice_a: Is always lower than the interest rate
choice_b: Only applies to adjustable-rate loans
choice_c: Is set by the Federal Reserve for every loan nationwide
choice_d: Reflects the interest rate plus certain other finance charges (such as points and some fees), expressed as a yearly rate
explanation: APR incorporates the interest rate along with certain prepaid finance charges, giving borrowers a more complete picture of the loan's true cost, and is typically higher than the stated note rate.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The Truth in Lending Act is implemented through federal regulations known as:
choice_a: Regulation Z
choice_b: Regulation X
choice_c: Regulation D
choice_d: Regulation B
explanation: Regulation Z, issued by the Federal Reserve Board and now administered by the CFPB, implements TILA's disclosure and substantive requirements.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: If the APR on a loan becomes inaccurate beyond the tolerance allowed by Regulation Z before closing, the lender generally must:
choice_a: Proceed to closing without any changes
choice_b: Provide a corrected Closing Disclosure and, in most cases, allow a new three-business-day waiting period before consummation
choice_c: Cancel the loan permanently
choice_d: Report the borrower to the CFPB
explanation: A change that causes the APR to become inaccurate beyond the applicable tolerance is a "changed circumstance" requiring a corrected Closing Disclosure and a new three-business-day waiting period.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: TRID's Loan Estimate/Closing Disclosure requirements generally do NOT apply to:
choice_a: A purchase-money mortgage on a single-family home
choice_b: A refinance of an owner-occupied residence
choice_c: Loans made primarily for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes, and loans secured by investment property
choice_d: Home equity loans secured by a principal residence
explanation: TRID's integrated disclosures apply to most closed-end consumer credit transactions secured by real property; business-purpose loans and certain investment property loans are excluded.
source_note: 12 CFR § 1026.19(e)(1); Official Interpretations to Regulation Z.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under Regulation Z's advertising rules, if an advertisement for credit states a specific 'triggering term' such as the amount of the down payment or number of payments, the ad must also:
choice_a: Include no additional information
choice_b: Be approved in advance by HUD
choice_c: Be limited to print media only
choice_d: Include all required additional credit disclosures, such as the APR
explanation: Regulation Z requires that if an advertisement includes certain triggering terms (down payment amount, number of payments, payment amount, or repayment period), it must also include full disclosure of the finance terms, including the APR.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The Sherman Antitrust Act primarily prohibits:
choice_a: Contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that unreasonably restrain trade, and monopolization
choice_b: Discrimination based on a buyer's national origin
choice_c: Failure to disclose lead-based paint hazards
choice_d: Charging any commission above 3%
explanation: The Sherman Act (1890) is the foundational federal antitrust law; Section 1 bars restraints of trade formed by agreement, and Section 2 bars monopolization.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Two competing brokerages agree that they will both charge exactly 6% commission on all listings. This conduct constitutes:
choice_a: A legal marketing strategy
choice_b: Price fixing, a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act
choice_c: Steering, prohibited under the Fair Housing Act
choice_d: A permissible RESPA affiliated business arrangement
explanation: Horizontal agreements among competitors to fix commission rates are treated as per se illegal price fixing under Section 1 of the Sherman Act, regardless of whether the fixed price is "reasonable."
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; United States v. Foley, 598 F.2d 1323 (4th Cir. 1979) (real estate commission fixing).

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A group of brokers agrees to refuse to show listings from, or otherwise exclude, a discount brokerage from the local MLS in order to punish its lower commission model. This is an example of:
choice_a: Tying arrangement
choice_b: Legitimate self-regulation
choice_c: Group boycott, a per se Sherman Act violation
choice_d: Redlining
explanation: Concerted refusals to deal — group boycotts — aimed at excluding a competitor are treated as per se illegal under the Sherman Act.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; FTC/DOJ antitrust guidance for real estate brokers.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Two brokerage firms agree that one will only operate in the northern half of the county and the other only in the southern half. This is known as:
choice_a: A permissible franchise territory agreement between unrelated competitors
choice_b: Blockbusting
choice_c: A RESPA-compliant referral arrangement
choice_d: Market allocation, a per se antitrust violation
explanation: Agreements between competitors to divide markets or territories eliminate competition between them and are per se illegal under the Sherman Act.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A brokerage requires that any buyer using its agents must also use its affiliated mortgage company in order to have their offer submitted. If this requirement stems from an anticompetitive agreement to eliminate competing lenders, it may constitute an illegal:
choice_a: Tying arrangement under the Sherman Act
choice_b: Reasonable accommodation under the ADA
choice_c: Disclosure under TILA
choice_d: Escrow requirement under RESPA
explanation: Tying arrangements — conditioning the sale of one product or service on the purchase of another — can violate the Sherman Act when they unreasonably restrain competition in the tied market.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act can result in which of the following consequences?
choice_a: Only a written warning from HUD
choice_b: Criminal fines and imprisonment for individuals, and civil treble damages recoverable by injured parties
choice_c: Suspension of the violator's real estate license only, with no other penalty
choice_d: No penalty for real estate licensees, since brokers are exempt
explanation: Sherman Act violations can be prosecuted criminally (fines and imprisonment) by the DOJ, and private parties injured by antitrust violations may sue for treble (triple) damages.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Federal antitrust enforcement of the Sherman Act is primarily carried out by:
choice_a: HUD's Office of Fair Housing
choice_b: State real estate commissions exclusively
choice_c: The Department of Justice Antitrust Division and the Federal Trade Commission
choice_d: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
explanation: The DOJ Antitrust Division and the FTC share responsibility for enforcing federal antitrust laws, including bringing actions against anticompetitive conduct in the real estate brokerage industry.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Which of the following is legal under the Sherman Antitrust Act?
choice_a: Competing brokers meeting to jointly set a standard commission rate
choice_b: Competing brokers agreeing to divide the MLS by geographic area
choice_c: Competing brokers agreeing to boycott a discount brokerage
choice_d: A brokerage independently deciding, without agreement with competitors, what commission rate to charge its clients
explanation: A firm's unilateral, independent decision about its own pricing is lawful; antitrust liability requires an agreement or concerted action among competitors to restrain trade.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1 (requires concerted action, not unilateral conduct).

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The federal Fair Housing Act, as amended, prohibits discrimination in housing based on which seven protected classes?
choice_a: Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability
choice_b: Race, color, age, income, marital status, sexual orientation, and religion
choice_c: Race, religion, sex, national origin, source of income, occupation, and age
choice_d: Color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, and criminal history
explanation: Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (the Fair Housing Act), as amended by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, protects race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability (handicap).
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A real estate agent who consistently shows minority home buyers properties only in certain neighborhoods, while showing other buyers a broader range of neighborhoods, is engaging in a discriminatory practice known as:
choice_a: Blockbusting
choice_b: Steering
choice_c: Redlining
choice_d: Panic peddling exemption
explanation: Steering is the practice of directing homebuyers toward or away from certain neighborhoods based on a protected characteristic, violating the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a); HUD Fair Housing enforcement guidance.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Persuading homeowners to sell quickly, often at a reduced price, by suggesting that the entry of a protected class into the neighborhood will lower property values, is a prohibited practice called:
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Tying
choice_c: Blockbusting (panic peddling)
choice_d: Constructive eviction
explanation: Blockbusting, or panic peddling, involves inducing sales by exploiting racial or other fears about a neighborhood's changing composition, and is prohibited under the Fair Housing Act.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A bank's practice of refusing to make mortgage loans, or offering less favorable terms, in neighborhoods based primarily on the racial or ethnic composition of the area, rather than the creditworthiness of individual applicants, is known as:
choice_a: Steering
choice_b: A legitimate underwriting practice
choice_c: Tying
choice_d: Redlining
explanation: Redlining refers to denying or limiting financial services, such as mortgage lending, to residents of certain areas based on race or ethnicity rather than individual creditworthiness, and it violates both the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, a real estate advertisement that states a preference such as 'no children' or 'Christian family preferred' is generally:
choice_a: Prohibited as discriminatory advertising indicating a preference based on a protected class
choice_b: Permitted as free speech
choice_c: Permitted if the seller personally requests the wording
choice_d: Only prohibited if published in a newspaper, not online
explanation: The Fair Housing Act prohibits advertisements that indicate a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class, regardless of the medium used.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD Advertising Guidelines, 24 CFR Part 109.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The limited Fair Housing Act exemption sometimes called the 'Mrs. Murphy exemption' applies to:
choice_a: Any landlord who owns fewer than 100 units nationwide
choice_b: Owner-occupied buildings with no more than four units, provided the owner does not use a broker or discriminatory advertising
choice_c: All single-family rentals regardless of who manages them
choice_d: Real estate brokers who personally reside in the listed property
explanation: This narrow exemption applies to owner-occupied dwellings of four units or fewer where the owner does not use a real estate agent or discriminatory advertising; it does not exempt race discrimination under the separate Civil Rights Act of 1866.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The Fair Housing Act provides a limited exemption allowing which of the following to give preference to their own members, under certain conditions?
choice_a: Commercial banks
choice_b: Franchised real estate brokerages
choice_c: Religious organizations and private clubs, for non-commercial lodgings they own or operate
choice_d: Title insurance companies
explanation: Religious organizations and bona fide private clubs may limit occupancy or give preference to their own members under narrow statutory exemptions, so long as membership is not restricted by race, color, or national origin.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A person who believes they have been the victim of housing discrimination generally must file a complaint with HUD within how long of the alleged discriminatory act, or file a lawsuit in federal court within how long?
choice_a: 30 days to file with HUD; 90 days to sue
choice_b: 5 years to file with HUD; 10 years to sue
choice_c: There is no time limit under federal law
choice_d: 1 year to file with HUD; 2 years to sue in federal court
explanation: Fair Housing Act complaints must generally be filed with HUD within one year of the discriminatory act, while a private civil action may be filed in federal court within two years.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The Fair Housing Act's protection for 'familial status' generally protects households with children under 18, but housing may be exempt from this specific protection if it qualifies as housing for older persons, meaning:
choice_a: Housing meeting HUD criteria such as 100% occupancy by residents 62 or older, or at least 80% of units having one resident 55 or older with required policies and verification
choice_b: Any apartment complex that simply advertises as 'adult living'
choice_c: Any building built before 1978
choice_d: Any housing where the landlord personally prefers not to rent to families
explanation: HUD regulations set specific criteria for the "housing for older persons" exemption (62-and-older or 55-and-older communities meeting occupancy, policy, and verification requirements) under the Housing for Older Persons Act.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b); Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995; 24 CFR Part 100, Subpart E.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, a landlord's refusal to waive a 'no pets' policy for a tenant who needs a service animal because of a disability, absent undue hardship, would likely violate the Act's requirement to provide:
choice_a: A structural modification at the landlord's sole expense in all cases
choice_b: A reasonable accommodation
choice_c: A rent reduction
choice_d: An exemption under ADA Title III only
explanation: The Fair Housing Act requires housing providers to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, or practices when necessary to afford persons with disabilities equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B); Joint HUD/DOJ Statement on Reasonable Accommodations.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, covered multifamily dwellings of four or more units designed and constructed for first occupancy after March 13, 1991, must include certain accessibility features. This requirement is known as the Act's:
choice_a: Reasonable modification provision
choice_b: Steering prohibition
choice_c: Design and construction requirements
choice_d: Blockbusting exemption
explanation: The FHAA's design and construction requirements mandate specific accessibility features (accessible entrances, usable doors, accessible routes, reinforced bathroom walls, etc.) in covered multifamily housing built after March 13, 1991.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), as distinguished from the Fair Housing Act, primarily applies to:
choice_a: Private, owner-occupied single-family residences
choice_b: Only federally subsidized housing
choice_c: Only new home construction
choice_d: Places of public accommodation and commercial facilities, such as real estate offices open to the public
explanation: While the Fair Housing Act governs residential dwellings, the ADA (Title III) governs accessibility in places of public accommodation and commercial facilities, including real estate brokerage offices.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: The federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act (Title X) and its implementing disclosure rule apply to the sale or lease of housing:
choice_a: Built before 1978
choice_b: Built at any time, regardless of age
choice_c: Built after 1978 only
choice_d: Only housing that is currently vacant
explanation: Because lead-based paint for residential use was banned in 1978, the federal disclosure rule applies to "target housing" built before that year.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Before a purchase contract becomes binding on pre-1978 housing, federal law requires the seller to:
choice_a: Remove all lead-based paint from the property
choice_b: Disclose known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards, provide any available reports, distribute the EPA pamphlet, and give the buyer a 10-day opportunity to conduct a risk assessment or inspection
choice_c: Provide a certified appraisal showing no lead contamination
choice_d: Obtain a permit from the EPA prior to listing the property
explanation: The federal disclosure rule requires sellers of pre-1978 housing to disclose known lead hazards/reports, provide the EPA's "Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home" pamphlet, and give buyers (unless waived) a 10-day period to test for lead.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Which of the following properties is generally EXEMPT from the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements?
choice_a: A single-family home built in 1965
choice_b: A duplex built in 1970
choice_c: Housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities, provided no children under age 6 reside there
choice_d: A rental unit built in 1972
explanation: Federal lead disclosure rules exempt certain categories such as housing exclusively for the elderly/disabled with no resident children under six, 0-bedroom efficiency units, and foreclosure sales.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under CERCLA (the federal Superfund law), liability for cleaning up a contaminated property can be imposed on the current owner even if that owner did not cause the contamination, because CERCLA imposes:
choice_a: Liability only on the original polluter
choice_b: No liability unless the owner is found criminally negligent
choice_c: Liability limited strictly to a percentage of the owner's involvement
choice_d: Strict, joint and several, and potentially retroactive liability on responsible parties, including current owners
explanation: CERCLA imposes strict liability (no fault required), joint and several liability (any one responsible party can be held liable for the whole cleanup), and can reach conduct that predates the statute.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A buyer of commercial property can potentially qualify for CERCLA's 'innocent landowner' defense to environmental cleanup liability if, before purchase, they conducted:
choice_a: 'All appropriate inquiries,' typically satisfied by a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment
choice_b: A home inspection only
choice_c: A title search only
choice_d: No due diligence is required for this defense
explanation: To preserve the innocent landowner (or bona fide prospective purchaser) defense under CERCLA, a purchaser must conduct "all appropriate inquiries" into prior ownership and uses, commonly satisfied through a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment meeting ASTM/EPA standards.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Regarding asbestos in residential real estate, which statement is most accurate under federal law?
choice_a: Federal law requires a standardized asbestos disclosure form for every home sale, similar to the lead-paint rule
choice_b: There is no comprehensive federal law mandating residential asbestos disclosure comparable to the lead-paint rule, though sellers may not misrepresent known conditions and specific federal rules (e.g., AHERA) target schools
choice_c: All asbestos-containing homes must be demolished under federal law
choice_d: The EPA bans the sale of any home containing asbestos
explanation: Unlike lead-based paint, there is no broad federal residential asbestos disclosure statute; AHERA specifically addresses asbestos in schools, and general anti-fraud/misrepresentation principles still apply to sellers who have actual knowledge.
source_note: Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act (AHERA), 15 U.S.C. § 2641 et seq. (schools); general state/federal disclosure principles.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under the federal Clean Water Act, a landowner who wants to discharge dredged or fill material into a wetland to develop the property must typically first obtain:
choice_a: Approval from the local homeowners association only
choice_b: A variance from the county zoning board only
choice_c: A Section 404 permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
choice_d: No permit is required if the land is privately owned
explanation: Section 404 of the Clean Water Act requires a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (in coordination with the EPA) before dredged or fill material may be discharged into wetlands or other jurisdictional waters.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Under the National Flood Insurance Program, a lender making a federally backed mortgage loan on a property located in a Special Flood Hazard Area must:
choice_a: Refuse to make the loan under any circumstances
choice_b: Automatically waive flood insurance if the buyer requests it
choice_c: Only require flood insurance for commercial properties
choice_d: Require the borrower to purchase and maintain flood insurance for the life of the loan
explanation: The NFIP, administered by FEMA, requires lenders to mandate flood insurance on federally related loans secured by improved property in a designated Special Flood Hazard Area (100-year floodplain).
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 4012a (Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973, as amended); NFIP regulations, 44 CFR Parts 59-64.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Regarding radon gas, which statement best reflects federal law and policy?
choice_a: The federal Indoor Radon Abatement Act set a national goal for indoor radon levels and EPA provides testing/mitigation guidance, but there is no general federal mandate requiring radon testing or disclosure in private home sales
choice_b: Federal law requires every home seller to test for radon and disclose the results before closing
choice_c: Radon is regulated exclusively by CERCLA
choice_d: Radon testing is banned by the EPA due to its unreliability
explanation: The Indoor Radon Abatement Act of 1988 established a national long-term goal for indoor radon levels and EPA guidance, but there is no comprehensive federal statute requiring radon testing or disclosure in ordinary residential sales (some states impose their own requirements).
source_note: Indoor Radon Abatement Act of 1988, 15 U.S.C. § 2661 et seq.; EPA "A Citizen's Guide to Radon."

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: Which statement most accurately reflects the federal regulatory landscape for mold in residential real estate?
choice_a: Mold is comprehensively regulated by a dedicated federal statute similar to the lead-paint disclosure rule
choice_b: There is no specific federal law regulating residential mold; concerns are generally addressed through state disclosure requirements, habitability standards, and general negligence principles, with HUD providing healthy-homes guidance
choice_c: CERCLA specifically designates all mold as a hazardous substance requiring Superfund cleanup
choice_d: Mold disclosure is required only for properties financed with VA loans
explanation: Unlike lead-based paint, no specific federal statute mandates residential mold disclosure or remediation; mold issues are typically handled at the state level and through general disclosure and habitability law, supplemented by HUD/EPA guidance documents.
source_note: HUD Healthy Homes Program guidance; absence of a dedicated federal mold statute.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A proposed subdivision development is found to be within the habitat of a federally listed endangered species. Under the Endangered Species Act, this discovery could most directly impact the project because the Act:
choice_a: Automatically prohibits any development anywhere in the same county
choice_b: Only applies to federally owned land, never private land
choice_c: Prohibits the 'take' of a listed species (including significant habitat modification that harms the species) and may require consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service before federal approvals are granted
choice_d: Has no bearing on private land use decisions
explanation: ESA Section 9 prohibits the "take" of listed species, which has been interpreted to include habitat modification causing harm, and Section 7 requires federal agencies to consult with the Fish and Wildlife Service (or NMFS) before authorizing, funding, or carrying out actions affecting listed species, which can constrain development requiring federal permits.

topic: Federal Laws Governing Real Estate Activities
question: A prospective commercial buyer wants to minimize the risk of inheriting CERCLA cleanup liability and identify other environmental red flags (such as underground storage tanks or wetlands) before closing. The standard industry practice used to investigate a property's environmental condition and support the innocent landowner defense is:
choice_a: A termite inspection
choice_b: A home warranty
choice_c: A preliminary title report
choice_d: A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA)
explanation: A Phase I ESA — a historical and physical review of a property for evidence of contamination — is the standard due diligence tool used to satisfy CERCLA's "all appropriate inquiries" requirement and to flag issues such as underground storage tanks, wetlands, or prior industrial use.
source_note: 40 CFR Part 312; ASTM E1527 standard practice for Phase I ESAs.
